Lives · 1914–2009

Norman Borlaug

Agriculture · United States · 1914–2009

2 min readWhere it is contestedCorrected onceUpdated 19 September 2026
On this pageWhere it is contestedCorrectedThe definitive biographyReads across to

Frequently called the man who saved more human lives than anyone who has ever lived — and most people have never heard of him.

If you keep one line

Applied science, done patiently in a field, can change the fate of nations.

ShareEmailXLinkedIn

An Iowa farm boy and plant pathologist, Borlaug spent the 1940s and 50s in Mexico. He crossbred thousands of wheat varieties. The goal was high-yielding, disease-resistant, short-stalked strains that could carry heavy heads of grain without toppling.

When famine threatened India and Pakistan in the 1960s, his wheat — paired with modern methods — roughly doubled harvests within years. Looming mass starvation turned into self-sufficiency. This was the Green Revolution, and it spread across Asia and Latin America.

He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970. He spent his remaining decades fighting hunger in Africa and defending agricultural science against critics, while acknowledging the environmental trade-offs of intensive farming. Borlaug is the quiet patron saint of the idea that applied science, done patiently in the field, can change the fate of nations.

01Where it is contested

An authorized biography by a colleague is not an independent one. The 'saved a billion lives' figure is repeated everywhere and calculated nowhere the house could find, so this entry does not print it; how many lives the Green Revolution saved is argued, not measured. The critics — on water depletion, fertiliser runoff, seed dependency and the concentration of gains among larger landholders — make arguments Hesser does not seriously engage. Both the achievement and the critique are real.

02Corrected

Corrections are appended, never patched. What was wrong, and what is true now:

№ 11 · Sept 2026 · Borlaug's billion and the Jobs paternity test.

Norman Borlaug's entry said estimates of the lives the Green Revolution saved run to a billion or more. The figure is repeated everywhere, and the house found no published calculation behind it; the entry on Tu Youyou already refused the same kind of number. It is gone from Borlaug's entry, and his contested section now says the scale is argued rather than measured. Steve Jobs' entry put the probability of paternity at 94.1 per cent, the figure usually cited to Time in 1983, which the house has not opened. Lisa Brennan-Jobs gives 94.4 per cent in her memoir, and the entry now prints hers, with the source named.

03The definitive biography

The Man Who Fed the WorldLeon Hesser · 2006

Hesser, an agricultural economist who worked alongside Borlaug in Pakistan, wrote the authorized biography with first-hand knowledge of the work. Warmly written and the fullest popular account.

04Reads across to

Fritz Haber — none of Borlaug's yields exist without Haber's nitrogen. The two entries are one story.

Maurice Hilleman — the same arithmetic, in vaccines rather than wheat.

Tu Youyou — artemisinin, found inside a secret military programme and credited, contentiously, to one person.
